questions.question: Why does Go return (value, error) pairs?
questions.title: Es Go Return (value, Error) Pairs
questions.direct_answer: Errors are values. The signature documents what can fail; the caller must handle it at the call site; multiple returns make the pairing natural.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
What makes the pattern work is a set of small language decisions acting together:

1. Multiple return values — the pair is expressible at all.
2. The error interface — one method, any type can implement it, so failures can be as rich as needed.
3. Unused-variable checking — you can't get the value without at least acknowledging the error slot (using _ on it is an explicit choice, not an accident).
4. No exceptions — there is no competing failure channel, so the visible one is the real one.

The contrast with exception languages isn't verbosity so much as where the knowledge lives. A Java caller of a throwing method must read the docs to know it throws; the compiler enforces catch-or-declare but not understanding. A Go caller sees the error in the signature and handles it or visibly discards it. The information moved from prose to types.

The payoff shows in code review: a reviewer can see every failure path of a Go function by reading it. With exceptions, the same review needs the whole call graph. That's the deep reason Go chose this — not terseness, but auditability of failure.

questions.question: What are the conventions for the error return value?
questions.title: Re The Conventions For The Error Return
questions.direct_answer: error is last; on failure, other values are zero/nil; on success, error is nil. Check err before using other values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Multiple Return Error.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: error is last; on failure, other values are zero/nil; on success, error is nil.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The conventions are stable enough that the whole ecosystem can rely on them:

The error, when present, is the last return value. Not second-of-three or configurable — last. Every Go programmer reads (bytes, err) and (n int, err error) the same way because the position never varies.

On failure, the other return values should be their zero values — nil, 0, empty. This lets callers use one guard: check err first, and if it's non-nil, don't trust anything else. A function that returns a partial result AND an error splits the convention and forces callers to read docs. Don't do it: on error, return nil for the rest.

On success, error is nil. Not 'nil sometimes with a warning' — nil means the other values are valid.

And the check order: err first, because reading other values before the check is the classic bug — a failed read may return a stale or zero count that the caller then acts on. The if err != nil guard at the top of the handling block isn't ceremony; it's the sequencing that keeps invalid data from flowing.

```go
// error is LAST; on failure, others are zero/nil; check err FIRST
data, err := os.ReadFile(path)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err           // nil result + error — the convention
}
return data, nil              // valid data + nil error
```

questions.question: Can a function return multiple errors?
questions.title: Can A Function Return Multiple Errors
questions.direct_answer: Idiomatically one. Go 1.20's errors.Join(err...) wraps several into a single error that errors.Is-matches each component.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Multiple Return Error.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Idiomatically one.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    E1[err task1] --> J[errors.Join]
    E2[err task2] --> J
    E3[err task3] --> J
    J --> ONE[one error — Is matches ANY component]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why was this added to the standard library in 2023 after a decade of one-error returns? Because the batch pattern had converged on private reimplementations. Everyone running parallel validation — form field checks, linters, CI steps, fan-out requests — hit the same wall: the first error is a subset of the truth, and swallowing the rest makes the caller iterate one-fix-one-round-trip. The multi-error structure shows up in enough places that the pattern deserved one shared implementation with correct Is/As semantics (a hand-rolled version usually gets the unwrap walk wrong).

The semantics that make Join correct: errors.Is(joinedErr, anyComponent) is true for each component; errors.As extracts each component type; the message joins all. The subtle part is nil handling — Join filters out nil components, and Join() with all-nils returns nil, so the builder pattern above doesn't need a nil guard.

The remaining guidance: one error return is still the default. Join is for genuinely parallel, independent failures. Sequential code (open file, parse it, save it) should still return the first error — the later steps didn't run, so reporting them as failures would be fiction.

questions.question: What is the blank identifier's role with errors?
questions.title: Blank Identifier's Role With Errors
questions.direct_answer: _, err := f() takes only the error; v, _ := f() ignores the error. The second is a lint smell — you lose the failure signal silently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Multiple Return Error.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: _, err := f() takes only the error; v, _ := f() ignores the error.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The blank identifier is how you opt out of one side of the (value, error) pair explicitly. `_, err := f()` says 'I need only the error' — common when you only care whether something succeeded. `v, _ := f()` says 'I need only the value, ignore the error' — and that second form deserves scrutiny.

Ignoring an error is sometimes correct: a best-effort cache write, a metrics flush, a debug log where failure changes nothing. In those cases `_` documents the decision at the call site — a reader sees that the error was considered and deliberately dropped, not overlooked.

But most `v, _ :=` calls are bugs in waiting. The failure the error reported doesn't disappear; it moves downstream — the zero value gets used, and the real cause becomes a mystery later ('why is this config empty?', 'why did nothing get written?'). The compiler accepted it silently, no test caught it, and production is where it surfaces. That's why linters flag discarded errors by default: the pattern is legal but the justification should be local and visible.

The middle path: don't ignore, log. `v, err := f(); if err != nil { log.Printf("...: %v", err) }` — three lines that convert a silent failure into a diagnosable one. Use `_` only where you can say, out loud, why the error doesn't matter.

```go
_, err := os.Stat(path)  // value unused; error kept — fine
v, _ := risky()          // error DISCARDED — the lint smell
v, err := risky(); if err != nil { log.Printf("%v", err) }  // honest
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanism is worth one layer down: the blank identifier is a write-only pseudo-variable. You can assign to it as many times as you like, read from it never. For the (value, error) contract, it's the explicit release valve — Go requires you to handle unused returns, and `_` is how you say 'unused on purpose.'

The interesting asymmetry: `_, err :=` is almost always fine (you want the error; the value being zero on failure is irrelevant), while `v, _ :=` is the one that hides bugs. The direction matters because the error is the signal and the value is the payload — discarding the payload is harmless when the signal says the payload is absent; discarding the signal means the payload's absence will surprise you.

The enforcement history explains the ecosystem's stance: Go's compiler checks unused VARIABLES but not unused return values in general — the single-return-value assignment would be an error, but multi-return with `_` never is. That gap between 'the language lets me' and 'the ecosystem expects' is exactly what errcheck-style linters filled. When a language leaves a discipline to convention, the convention grows teeth as tooling.

questions.question: How does the (T, error) pattern affect API design?
questions.title: Es The (t, Error) Pattern Affect Api
questions.direct_answer: It forces explicit failure modeling: every call site answers 'what happens if this fails?' — visible branches instead of hidden throws.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Multiple Return Error.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: It forces explicit failure modeling: every call site answers 'what happens if this fails?' — visible branches instead.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The pattern shapes APIs before any implementation exists. When you design a function that can fail, Go's signature forces the question: what does the caller get back on failure? A (T, error) return says 'you might get nothing but an explanation.' The signature is the contract, and it's impossible to add a failure mode later without changing it — every caller sees and adapts. Compare adding a new thrown exception in another language: existing callers find out when it flies past them at runtime.

This pushes toward a particular style of API: fewer things that 'sometimes fail silently,' more small operations with clear failure contracts. Constructors become pairs — NewX() (X, error) — and the zero-value-vs-validation debate (make invalid states unrepresentable vs a usable zero value) plays out in every design.

It also standardizes the caller's shape. Every consumer of a fallible API has the same skeleton — call, check, wrap-or-handle — so teams can read each other's failure paths fluently. The uniformity is the point: a Go codebase reads like one style of error handling, not N personal ones.

```go
// the signature IS the failure contract:
func Load(path string) (Config, error)  // can fail — caller sees it
func NewBuffer() *bytes.Buffer           // zero value usable — can't fail

// callers cannot ignore the failure without writing _:
cfg, _ := Load(path)  // the _ is a visible choice, flagged by linters
```
